paragraphs.text: When offices around the world closed in 2020, millions of employees began working from home almost overnight. Many organisations expected productivity to collapse. Instead, early surveys suggested that most workers felt they were achieving as much as before, or more. The question that has occupied economists since then is whether those feelings reflected reality.

One of the most influential studies was carried out years before the pandemic. In 2013, the Stanford economist Nicholas Bloom ran an experiment with a Chinese travel company, randomly assigning call-centre staff either to work from home or to remain in the office. Those at home were 13% more productive, mainly because they took fewer breaks and sick days and worked in a quieter environment. However, about half of them chose to return to the office when given the option, citing loneliness.

Later research produced more mixed results. A 2023 study by Natalia Emanuel and Emma Harrington of software engineers at a large American company found that working remotely reduced the amount of feedback junior employees received from more experienced colleagues. In the short term, output was unaffected, but the researchers warned that the long-term development of young staff could suffer. In my view, this is the most serious weakness of fully remote work, and one that is easily overlooked because it does not appear in productivity figures.

Other studies have focused on creativity. Research led by Melanie Brucks, comparing pairs of people who brainstormed ideas either in person or by video call, found that the video groups generated fewer creative ideas, possibly because staring at a screen narrows attention. It would be wrong, though, to conclude that remote meetings are always inferior; the same study found no difference when the groups had to choose the best idea.

Most companies have now settled on hybrid arrangements, typically with two or three days a week in the office. A 2024 study by Bloom of a large technology firm found that hybrid workers were just as productive as office workers and considerably less likely to resign. Hybrid working, I believe, offers the most sensible compromise for most organisations, although the right balance will vary between jobs.
